entry.title: Efficient Maximum Likelihood Estimation of Multiple Membership Linear Mixed Models, with an Application to Educational Value-Added Assessments

link.title: Efficient Maximum Likelihood Estimation of Multiple Membership Linear Mixed Models, with an Application to Educational Value-Added Assessments

entry.content: The generalized persistence (GP) model, developed in the context of estimating ``value added’’ by individual teachers to their students’ current and future test scores, is one of the most flexible value-added models in the literature. Although developed in the educational setting, the GP model can potentially be applied to any structure where each sequential response of a lower-level unit may be associated with a different higher-level unit, and the effects of the higher-level units may persist over time. The flexibility of the GP model, however, and its multiple membership random effects structure lead to computational challenges that have limited the model’s availability. We develop an EM algorithm to compute maximum likelihood estimates efficiently for the GP model, making use of the sparse structure of the random effects and error covariance matrices. The algorithm is implemented in the package GPvam in R statistical software. We give examples of the computations and illustrate the gains in computational efficiency achieved by our estimation procedure.

entry.title: Avoiding Bias Due to Nonrandom Scheduling When Modeling Trends in Home-Field Advantage

link.title: Avoiding Bias Due to Nonrandom Scheduling When Modeling Trends in Home-Field Advantage

entry.content: Existing approaches for estimating home-field advantage (HFA) include modeling the difference between home and away scores as a function of the difference between home and away team ratings that are treated either as fixed or random effects. We uncover an upward bias in the mixed model HFA estimates that can arise when the schedule – and thus the random effect design matrix – depends on team strengths, and explore why the fixed effects model is not subject to the same bias. Intraconference HFAs and standard errors are calculated for each of 3 college sports and 3 professional sports over the 2000-2017 seasons and then fitted with conference-specific slopes and intercepts to measure the potential linear population trend in HFA.

entry.title: A Randomized Permutation Whole-Model Test Heuristic for Self-Validated Ensemble Models (SVEM)

link.title: A Randomized Permutation Whole-Model Test Heuristic for Self-Validated Ensemble Models (SVEM)

entry.content: We introduce a heuristic to test the significance of fit of Self-Validated Ensemble Models (SVEM) against the null hypothesis of a constant response. A SVEM model averages predictions from nBoot fits of a model, applied to fractionally weighted bootstraps of the target dataset. It tunes each fit on a validation copy of the training data, utilizing anti-correlated weights for training and validation. The proposed test computes SVEM predictions centered by the response column mean and normalized by the ensemble variability at each of nPoint points spaced throughout the factor space. A reference distribution is constructed by refitting the SVEM model to nPerm randomized permutations of the response column and recording the corresponding standardized predictions at the nPoint points. A reduced-rank singular value decomposition applied to the centered and scaled nPerm x nPoint reference matrix is used to calculate the Mahalanobis distance for each of the nPerm permutation results as well as the jackknife (holdout) Mahalanobis distance of the original response column. The process is repeated independently for each response in the experiment, producing a joint graphical summary. We present a simulation driven power analysis and discuss limitations of the test relating to model flexibility and design adequacy. The test maintains the nominal Type I error rate even when the base SVEM model contains more parameters than observations.

entry.title: Bayesian nonparametric mixtures of Archimedean copulas

link.title: Bayesian nonparametric mixtures of Archimedean copulas

entry.content: Copula-based dependence modeling often relies on parametric formulations. This is mathematically convenient, but can be statistically inefficient when the parametric families are not suitable for the data and model in focus. A Bayesian nonparametric mixture of Archimedean copulas is introduced to increase the flexibility of copula-based dependence modeling. Specifically, the Poisson-Dirichlet process is used as a mixing distribution over the Archimedean copulas’ parameter. Properties of the mixture model are studied for the main Archimedean families, and posterior distributions are sampled via their full conditional distributions. The performance of the model is illustrated via numerical experiments involving simulated and real data.

entry.title: Selection from Hierarchical Data with Conformal e-values

link.title: Selection from Hierarchical Data with Conformal e-values

entry.content: Distribution-free predictive inference beyond the construction of prediction sets has gained a lot of interest in recent applications. One such application is the selection task, where the objective is to design a reliable selection rule to pick out individuals with desired unobserved outcomes while controlling the error rate. In this work, we address the selection problem in the context of hierarchical data, where groups of observations may exhibit distinct within-group distributions. This generalizes existing techniques beyond the standard i.i.d./exchangeable data settings. As a correction, For hierarchical data, we introduce methods to construct valid conformal e-values, enabling control of the false discovery rate (FDR) through the e-BH procedure. In particular, we introduce and compare two approaches – subsampling conformal e-values and hierarchical conformal e-values. Empirical results demonstrate that both approaches achieve valid FDR control while highlighting a tradeoff between stability and power. The subsampling-based method, though random, typically offers higher power, whereas the hierarchical approach, being deterministic, tends to be slightly less powerful. The effectiveness of the proposed methods is illustrated in two real-world applications.

entry.title: How Much Weak Overlap Can Doubly Robust T-Statistics Handle?

link.title: How Much Weak Overlap Can Doubly Robust T-Statistics Handle?

entry.content: Propensity scores near zero or one can make standard confidence intervals undercover. Econometric theory has targeted the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) under such weak overlap using nonstandard estimators or intervals. Practice has instead favored fixed thresholding rules that restore asymptotic normality by discarding extreme-propensity units for whom treatment may matter most. I show that standard t-tests for the ATE remain valid even when overlap is so weak that every regular estimator has infinite asymptotic variance. The key is to threshold the usual doubly robust estimator aggressively enough to control bias among unthresholded observations, but mildly enough to control bias from thresholding. I provide sufficient conditions for such thresholds to exist, and propose an adaptive rule of thumb to achieve coverage without knowing the weak overlap degree. In a canonical application, fixed trimming excludes 18% of the sample; the adaptive procedure estimates the resulting bias at five percent of the effect.

entry.title: Uniform ergodicity and spectral gap of importance-tempered MCMC with heavy-tailed targets

link.title: Uniform ergodicity and spectral gap of importance-tempered MCMC with heavy-tailed targets

entry.content: We study the importance-tempered random-walk Metropolis (RWM) algorithm on $\mathbb{R}^d$, which targets the tempered density $\pi_\beta(x) \propto \pi(x)^\beta$ with $\beta \in (0,1)$ and corrects for the resulting bias by importance weighting. The dynamics of this sampler can be described by a continuous-time Markov chain whose embedded chain is the tempered RWM. We prove that when the tails of $\pi$ decay at rate $|x|^{-\gamma}$, this continuous-time chain is uniformly ergodic if and only if $d/\gamma < \beta < (\gamma - 2)/\gamma$. Further, the global spectral gap of this chain can be controlled via the spectral gap of the chain restricted to a ball with radius growing polynomially in $d$. Our theory and simulation studies show that, with a suitable choice of $\beta$, importance tempering can substantially reduce sensitivity to initialization and significantly improve efficiency over the standard RWM.

entry.title: Conformalized Polynomial Chaos Expansion for Uncertainty-aware Surrogate Modeling

link.title: Conformalized Polynomial Chaos Expansion for Uncertainty-aware Surrogate Modeling

entry.content: This work introduces a method to equip data-driven polynomial chaos expansion surrogate models with intervals that quantify the predictive uncertainty of the surrogate. To that end, jackknife-based conformal prediction is integrated into regression-based polynomial chaos expansions. The jackknife algorithm uses leave-one-out residuals to generate predictive intervals around the predictions of the polynomial chaos surrogate. The jackknife+ extension additionally requires leave-one-out model predictions. Both methods allow to use the entire dataset for model training and do not require a hold-out dataset for prediction interval calibration. The key to efficient implementation is to leverage the linearity of the polynomial chaos regression model, so that leave-one-out residuals and, if necessary, leave-one-out model predictions can be computed with analytical, closed-form expressions. This eliminates the need for repeated model re-training. The conformalized polynomial chaos expansion method is first validated on four benchmark models and then applied to two electrical engineering design use-cases. The method produces predictive intervals that provide the target coverages, even for low-accuracy models trained with small datasets. At the same time, training data availability plays a crucial role in improving the empirical coverage and narrowing the predictive interval, as well as in reducing their variability over different training datasets.

entry.title: Universal Inference for Testing Calibration and Specification of Mean Estimates within the Exponential Dispersion Family

link.title: Universal Inference for Testing Calibration and Specification of Mean Estimates within the Exponential Dispersion Family

entry.content: Calibration of mean estimates is a crucial property in many applications, particularly in actuarial decision-making. Tests of mean-calibration are often performed under the assumption that the estimated means correctly preserve the ordering of the corresponding population means. In this paper, we first consider the classical Likelihood Ratio Test (LRT) within the Exponential Dispersion Family (EDF), and we show that applying likelihood-based methods to test mean-calibration within the EDF requires a strong ordering assumption on the mean estimates. This assumption makes the null hypothesis of the mean-calibration test equivalent to the correct specification of the mean estimates. Next, we investigate the framework of universal inference for testing mean-calibration and mean-specification, and the relationship between the tests. We develop a sub-sampled split LRT within the EDF that provides finite-sample guarantees with universally valid critical values. We investigate type I error, power, and e-power of the sub-sampled split LRT and compare its performance with that of the classical LRT. We also propose a novel test statistic based on a sub-sampled split $L_q$-likelihood ratio test (L$q$RT) to enhance the performance of the statistical test. Numerical results demonstrate that universal inference based on the sub-sampled split LRT and sub-sampled split L$q$RT provides an attractive alternative to the classical LRT within the EDF, achieving high power for detecting miscalibration and misspecification in medium- and large-sized samples.

entry.title: Entropy-Guided Greedy Heuristic for Minimal Differential Set Construction

link.title: Entropy-Guided Greedy Heuristic for Minimal Differential Set Construction

entry.content: This paper addresses the challenge of identifying a minimal subset of discrete predictor variables that best explains a binary class. We propose a greedy heuristic for feature selection that sequentially constructs a differential set by iteratively adding the variable that yields the most significant reduction in conditional entropy. The method incorporates a confidence-guided acceptance criterion that accounts for finite-sample uncertainty, allowing the search to adaptively balance the risk of including spurious variables against the opportunity to capture meaningful predictors. Because the procedure yields a compact set of statistically validated predictors together with an explicit confidence level for each one, it is well suited to healthcare innovation and management applications such as biomarker and risk-factor identification, diagnostic panel design, and clinical decision support, where minimizing the number of tests or indicators collected is critical for cost, feasibility, and patient burden.

entry.title: SVEMnet: An R package for Self-Validated Elastic-Net Ensembles and Multi-Response Optimization in Small-Sample Mixture-Process Experiments

link.title: SVEMnet: An R package for Self-Validated Elastic-Net Ensembles and Multi-Response Optimization in Small-Sample Mixture-Process Experiments

entry.content: SVEMnet is an R package for fitting Self-Validated Ensemble Models (SVEM) with elastic-net base learners and performing multi-response optimization in small-sample mixture-process design-of-experiments (DOE) studies with numeric, categorical, and mixture factors. SVEMnet wraps elastic-net and relaxed elastic-net models for Gaussian and binomial responses from glmnet in a fractional random-weight (FRW) resampling scheme with anti-correlated train/validation weights; penalties are selected by validation-weighted AIC- and BIC-type criteria, and predictions are averaged across replicates to stabilize fits near the interpolation boundary. In addition to the core SVEM engine, the package provides deterministic high-order formula expansion, a permutation-based whole-model test heuristic, and a mixture-constrained random-search optimizer that combines Derringer-Suich desirability functions, bootstrap-based uncertainty summaries, and optional mean-level specification-limit probabilities to generate scored candidate tables and diverse exploitation and exploration medoids for sequential fit-score-run-refit workflows. A simulated lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation study illustrates these tools in a small-sample mixture-process DOE setting, and simulation experiments based on sparse quadratic response surfaces benchmark SVEMnet against repeated cross-validated elastic-net baselines.

entry.title: NeuroMAS: Multi-Agent Systems as Neural Networks with Joint Reinforcement Learning

link.title: NeuroMAS: Multi-Agent Systems as Neural Networks with Joint Reinforcement Learning

entry.content: Multi-agent language systems are often built as hand-designed workflows, where agents are assigned semantic roles and communication protocols are specified in advance. We propose NeuroMAS, a method that first treats a multi-agent language system as a trainable and scalable neural-network-like architecture with LLM agents as nodes and intermediate textual signals as edges. In NeuroMAS, agent nodes are role-free but structure-aware: the topology only determines how information can flow in general, while reinforcement learning training determines how nodes communicate, specialize, and coordinate. This formulation shifts multi-agent design from workflow engineering toward architecture design, where depth, width, connectivity, and growth protocol become scalable sources of capability. Further, we provide a theoretical perspective showing why such modular textual computation is more parameter-efficient when tasks admit hierarchical decompositions. Experiments show that NeuroMAS improves significantly over both inference-time and trained multi-agent baselines. We further find that organizational scaling is path-dependent: larger systems can be challenging to train from scratch, but become feasible when grown progressively from smaller trained systems. These results suggest that learned neural multi-agent systems are a promising scaling axis for LLMs.

entry.title: Causal Representation Learning for Generalisable Recommendation

link.title: Causal Representation Learning for Generalisable Recommendation

entry.content: Predictive models trained on observational data often fail to generalise when deployed, especially when the training data is a product of the system being optimised. Recommender systems are a canonical example: they are trained on interaction logs confounded by the deployed policy, past user behaviour, and platform filtering. As a result, the training distribution differs from the candidate distribution scored at serving time, a gap that makes offline metrics unreliable predictors of online performance. We address the distribution shift problem with a method motivated by causal representation learning (CRL). We propose an information-theoretic disentanglement criterion and prove that its optimum excludes confounder-dependent non-causal information from the treatment representation. We derive a tractable variational lower bound making the criterion optimisable from finite observational data. The scope of our method is narrower than that of much of the CRL literature, in that we target better generalisation under distribution shift, not full identification of latent causal factors. This narrower target makes the method practical, requiring only existing confounded logs, applying to any standard supervised model, and adding no inference-time cost. Our headline evaluation is an A/B test with millions of users on Spotify, applied to a production ranker for personalised playlist generation. A CRL variant matched in capacity to the production baseline performed on par offline but delivered substantial online gains in listener engagement. Complementary evidence on a synthetic dataset with known causal structure and a semi-synthetic variant of the public KuaiRand recommendation dataset shows similar in-distribution performance to the baseline but gains under distribution shift. Across all three settings, adding our causal disentanglement objective yields better out-of-distribution generalisation.

entry.title: High-dimensional reliability-oriented Shapley effects estimation

link.title: High-dimensional reliability-oriented Shapley effects estimation

entry.content: This article presents a new estimation scheme for the reliability-oriented Shapley effects when there is a large number of correlated input variables, using a unique sample of failure points. First, we propose a new reformulation of the reliability-oriented closed Sobol indices. This reformulation circumvents the estimation issues associated with existing methods in the literature, but requires estimating densities in potentially high dimensions. Once the reliability-oriented closed Sobol indices have been estimated through these densities, the reliability-oriented Shapley effects are estimated through permutation aggregation to circumvent the issue related to the dimension. In addition, we provide an error estimation procedure relying on the same sample of failing points resulting in a probabilistic error bound, and avoiding any additional call to the model. We illustrate our methodology on numerical use-cases where we compare several density estimators and we propose an application to the monitoring of adaptive importance sampling.

entry.title: Weighted Extensions of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Cramer-von Mises, and Anderson-Darling Tests for Assessing Covariate Balance

link.title: Weighted Extensions of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Cramer-von Mises, and Anderson-Darling Tests for Assessing Covariate Balance

entry.content: Assessing covariate balance is central to causal inference, but commonly used summary measures may miss distributional differences. I develop weighted extensions of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS), Anderson-Darling (AD), and Cramer-von Mises (CVM) statistics and investigate their calibration when weights are externally supplied or estimated from treatment assignment. With exogenous weights, fixed-weight permutation produced approximately nominal Type I error. entry.title: Learning Bidirectional Causal Interactions with Heteroscedastic Neural Networks

link.title: Learning Bidirectional Causal Interactions with Heteroscedastic Neural Networks

entry.content: Estimating contemporaneous bidirectional interactions from observational data is difficult because each outcome is endogenous to the other, while flexible regressions may capture only reduced-form dependence. This paper proposes SEM-DNN, a heteroscedastic neural simultaneous-equation estimator that learns reciprocal structural interactions without external instruments. Identification exploits conditional covariance diagonalization: when structural shocks have zero conditional means, are conditionally uncorrelated given predetermined covariates, and exhibit nonproportional conditional variances, only the true interaction coefficients diagonalize the conditional residual covariance across the feature space. The method jointly approximates nonlinear structural mean functions and feature-dependent variances using a diagonal Gaussian quasi-likelihood that incorporates the simultaneous-system Jacobian. We establish unique identification and positive-definite local curvature of the profiled population criterion and show that, under neural-profile compatibility conditions, the implemented neural criterion inherits this curvature despite nonunique network parameterizations. The coefficients admit a causal interpretation when the structural equations represent autonomous mechanisms that remain invariant under the relevant interventions. Monte Carlo experiments with nonlinear, high-dimensional nuisance functions and non-Gaussian shocks show that SEM-DNN recovers structural effects more reliably than parametric, kernel-based, and separate-equation neural alternatives as information increases, although at greater computational cost. An application to ready-to-eat cereal scanner data illustrates how the method can study contemporaneous price-sales feedback and assess identification strength, residual diagonalization, variance calibration, and optimization sensitivity.

entry.title: Bayesian ACCESS for Understanding Latent Epidemic Trajectories from Publicly Released Suppressed Data: Application to U.S. Opioid-related Overdose Mortality

link.title: Bayesian ACCESS for Understanding Latent Epidemic Trajectories from Publicly Released Suppressed Data: Application to U.S. Opioid-related Overdose Mortality

entry.content: Publicly released health statistics play a central role in characterizing temporal trends and identifying structural changes in population health. However, disclosure limitation through suppression of small cell counts, as implemented in systems such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Wide-ranging ONline Data for Epidemiologic Research (CDC WONDER), produces partially observed count data that complicate statistical inference. These challenges are particularly acute for rare outcomes and subgroup analyses, where suppression is widespread and varies across geographic regions, demographic populations, and time. We propose Bayesian ACCESS (Autoregressive Change-point and Clustering Estimation for Suppressed Count Series), a Bayesian hierarchical framework for inference on latent epidemic trajectories and their structural changes from disclosure-limited health statistics. The proposed model directly represents suppressed count data through a suppression-aware observation model, jointly infers multiple temporal change points and latent trajectories, and borrows information across related geographic and demographic populations while preserving meaningful heterogeneity. We apply Bayesian ACCESS to opioid-related overdose mortality data from CDC WONDER for U.S. states from 1999 to 2024. The analysis identifies distinct subgroup-specific epidemic trajectories and structural changes that would be difficult to characterize using publicly released health statistics without explicitly accounting for data suppression and efficiently borrowing information across subgroups.

entry.title: SAUSS: Stochastic Approximation with Unbiased Simulated Scores for Limited Dependent Variable Models

link.title: SAUSS: Stochastic Approximation with Unbiased Simulated Scores for Limited Dependent Variable Models

entry.content: Simulated maximum likelihood is widely used in latent-variable models where likelihood evaluation requires intractable integrals or probabilities. With a fixed number of simulation draws, its estimating equation is generally biased. We develop Stochastic Approximation with Unbiased Simulated Scores (SAUSS), combining score simulation with stochastic gradient descent. The Hajivassiliou–McFadden identity, an instance of Fisher’s identity, expresses the likelihood score as the conditional expectation of the complete-data score given the observed data. Exact conditional draws yield an unbiased simulated score for any fixed number of draws. The estimator averages stochastic gradient iterates computed using mini-batches of fixed size regardless of sample size, avoiding repeated full-sample likelihood evaluations. Under local regularity and initialization conditions, we establish asymptotic normality and a functional central limit theorem for the partial-sum process of the iterates under multi-pass sampling from an observed sample. These results support plug-in and random-scaling confidence intervals that remain asymptotically valid when algorithmic uncertainty is non-negligible relative to sampling uncertainty. We develop multinomial probit as a leading application. In simulations and two applications, SAUSS returns estimates in every reported run, including cases where the simulated maximum likelihood implementation returns none. When both return estimates, SAUSS gives comparable estimates in less time.

entry.title: Second-order perturbation bounds for Gibbs samplers under strong spatial mixing

link.title: Second-order perturbation bounds for Gibbs samplers under strong spatial mixing

entry.content: The basic question in perturbation analysis of Markov chains is how small changes in their transition kernels affect their stationary distributions. Classical perturbation bounds typically require the kernel error to be much smaller than $1/\tau$, where $\tau$ is a mixing or relaxation time. Although this scaling is sharp for Markov chains in general, we investigate a general “square-rooting” phenomenon in which one-step errors of order roughly $1/\sqrt{\tau}$ can be sufficient for local updates. We proved a form of this phenomenon in Lin, Liu and Smith (2025) under strong assumptions. Here we substantially weaken these assumptions, and prove this phenomenon occurs using three distinct approaches. First, block factorization applies under structural assumptions on the stationary measures of both chains. Second, approximate block-update arguments extend the result to statistically relevant Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) settings, where structural guarantees are available for the exact posterior and its associated sampler, but not for the perturbed posterior. Third, we use direct calculations for a class of models with hard constraints where neither general result is directly available. We illustrate these results in three MCMC settings and show how they directly inform the tuning of approximate MCMC algorithms.

entry.title: The Geometry of Existence and Uniqueness of Maximum Likelihood Estimation in Categorical Response Models

link.title: The Geometry of Existence and Uniqueness of Maximum Likelihood Estimation in Categorical Response Models

entry.content: Nonexistence of the maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) under separation is treated as a solved problem for binary logistic regression and as a scattered collection of model-specific results everywhere else. We show that it is one phenomenon with one criterion. In a latent polyhedral categorical response model, every observed outcome corresponds to a polyhedral event in latent variables whose faces shift linearly with the parameter. Random-utility choice, cumulative-link, ranking, multivariate binary and ordinal, sequential, adjacent-category logit, and fixed-score stereotype models belong to this family. The likelihood sees each observed factor only through the columns of its threshold map, the structure vectors. A finite MLE exists if and only if the pooled structure vector set has overlap. Sufficiency requires only continuity, necessity requires only strictly threshold-increasing probabilities, and neither likelihood concavity, exchangeability, nor full design rank is needed. Positive strictly log-concave latent densities and threshold-identifiable polyhedra then yield uniqueness on the estimable span. A single linear program determines whether overlap holds, and convex cone geometry measures the dimension of separation. An application using cumulative-link models for willingness to share health data identifies observations and model terms associated with nonexistence and illustrates how the diagnostics inform model revision and sensitivity analysis.

entry.title: Prediction-Powered Data Fusion for Treatment Effect Estimation

link.title: Prediction-Powered Data Fusion for Treatment Effect Estimation

entry.content: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) identify treatment effects without confounding but are often small, whereas observational studies (OBS) are large but may be confounded. Many estimators combining a small RCT with a large OBS have been developed for the average treatment effect (ATE) and the conditional ATE (CATE). However, existing ATE estimators either make assumptions on the OBS or do not borrow enough power from them. The CATE has been studied less than the ATE. Existing CATE methods either assume the OBS are unconfounded, rely on a model of the confounding function, or accept bias in exchange for lower variance. We therefore propose a framework that, without special assumptions on the OBS, fuses the OBS and the RCT by preserving the unbiasedness of RCT-based estimation while borrowing power from the large OBS to boost precision. Applying this principle, we build an ATE estimator, AIPW-Fusion, with closed-form weights and confidence intervals, and two CATE learners, DR-Fusion and R-Fusion. Experiments corroborate our findings.

entry.title: Women and the Nobel Prize in the sciences: an update to 2026

link.title: Women and the Nobel Prize in the sciences: an update to 2026

entry.content: Every October, the Nobel Prizes in Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine and Economic Sciences are announced, with one to three prizes in each discipline. Of the 769 Laureates (since 1901) in these four disciplines only 4% are women (30 Laureates). In 2026, there are eight Laureates within these disciplines and they are all men. Based on historical data across four fields and a Bayesian hierarchical model, we update the 8 year old model on bias in Nobel Prizes and confirm the gender gap, with exceedingly large confidence.

entry.title: Where the Data End and the Mechanism Begins: Doubly Robust Causal Digital Twins for Treatment Strategies

link.title: Where the Data End and the Mechanism Begins: Doubly Robust Causal Digital Twins for Treatment Strategies

entry.content: Digital twins are increasingly used to ask how a patient’s health would evolve under alternative treatment strategies. When a twin couples a mechanistic model with learned components and is fitted to observational records, its answer mixes information from the data with assumptions from the mechanism. For sustained strategies that begin at a clinical landmark, we split the counterfactual mean into a part the data support, where patients follow the strategy with probability bounded away from zero, and a part they do not. On the supported part, a cross-fitted sequential doubly robust estimator that uses the twin as its outcome model is consistent whenever the decision model is, so twins that fit equally well but disagree as plug-in estimators agree after correction. On the unsupported part, we characterize the values compatible with the data and with a residual of size at most epsilon around the mechanism. This set is nested in epsilon, reduces to a point when the mechanism is exact and identifiable, and recovers assumption-free bounds as epsilon grows, so the penalty weight of a physics-informed loss becomes a sensitivity parameter. Knowledge constraints on how covariates enter the mechanism shrink the set, and when support grows over time, back-testing gives a data-based lower bound on epsilon. In simulations based on an energy-balance model of weight change under glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist therapy, the correction reduced the spread of estimates across four twins from 0.66 to 0.03 percentage points of weight loss with conservative coverage; on unsupported patients, the exact mechanism was rejected in every replicate, the bounds covered the truth at every residual size not rejected, and a mechanism-free extrapolation was biased by 0.5 points.

entry.title: Operationalising Weaker Faithfulness: Recovery, Ambiguity and Computational Limits

link.title: Operationalising Weaker Faithfulness: Recovery, Ambiguity and Computational Limits

entry.content: Variables can predict an outcome jointly while each is individually independent of it, causing structure learners to discard informative links. We investigate how to operationalise weaker faithfulness through two approaches: selective protection in an adjacency learner and explicit retention of alternative directed graph explanations. Matched experiments show that changes at both an early candidate-removal stage and later pruning can be necessary. In noisy XOR with a descendant (N = 10,000, 20 matched samples), combining reactivation and protection raises complete parent-pair recovery from 0/20 for either change alone to 20/20, while adding false edges. A confirmation study shows that the family estimator can preserve explanations lost by orienting the protected learner’s selected skeleton: in one weaker signal XOR condition (N = 10,000) it retains the entire reference family in 48/50 samples, compared with 0/50 for the skeleton adapter. These gains are conditional. Protection can add only error, weaker effects produce false exclusions, and an ordinary faithful-chain comparison favours the PC learner. Complete nonempty family outputs decline at six/eight variables, and all 400 twelve/twenty-variable searches remain unfinished at the reporting cutoff. Neural controls show engineered retention, while the family estimator returns no accepted graph within its application budget. This operationalisation identifies two deletion stages that must be coordinated in the motivating example and shows when direct family search preserves explanations lost by selecting one skeleton. Finite evidence and computation remain substantial barriers to reliable general inference.

entry.title: Changing contribution of a shared neighbourhood pattern to reported sexual and non-sexual violence against women and girls in Medellín, Colombia, 2018–2022

link.title: Changing contribution of a shared neighbourhood pattern to reported sexual and non-sexual violence against women and girls in Medellín, Colombia, 2018–2022

entry.content: During the COVID-19 restrictions, notifications of violence against women and girls may have changed unevenly across neighbourhoods. We asked whether the contribution of a shared neighbourhood pattern changed over this period, and whether any change was common to sexual and non-sexual violence or specific to one. We analysed 46,390 suspected cases notified to the public-health surveillance system of Medell'in, Colombia, across 285 neighbourhoods in 2018-2022. A Bayesian shared-component model with age-standardised expected counts allowed the loading of a common spatial field on each form of violence to differ between the pre-pandemic (2018-2019), restriction (2020-2021) and post-restriction (2022) periods. Across the urban communes, the shared field was generally higher where living conditions were poorer. During the restrictions, its loading increased by 0.26 (95% credible interval 0.16-0.37) for non-sexual violence and by 0.23 (0.09-0.37) for sexual violence, without clear evidence of a change in their ratio. Between neighbourhoods at the 90th and 10th percentiles of the shared field, the shared component’s contribution to their risk ratio widened by about 36% for non-sexual and 31% for sexual violence. In 2022, the non-sexual loading remained 0.19 (0.07-0.31) above its pre-pandemic value, whereas the sexual-violence loading was close to its pre-pandemic level. The direction of these changes was retained among notifications from health institutions only and under alternative specifications. Twenty-five neighbourhoods had joint probabilities above 0.95 of both relative risks exceeding one in all five years. The contribution of the shared neighbourhood pattern increased for both outcomes during the restrictions and remained elevated in 2022 for non-sexual violence.

entry.title: Hierarchical Absorbing Markov Chain Models for Pooling Sparse Combat Sequence Data

link.title: Hierarchical Absorbing Markov Chain Models for Pooling Sparse Combat Sequence Data

entry.content: By viewing tactics in no-gi Brazilian jiu-jitsu (NGJJ) as discrete states, we estimate the transition probabilities of tactical progression, while simultaneously exploring the effects of weight categories on these dynamics with a hierarchical absorbing Markov chain model. We further cluster the weight categories and borrow strength using the Ewens-Pitman attraction of Dahl, Day and Tsai. Random partitions allow us to explore the underlying groupings of these weight categories in terms of their transition patterns. The hierarchical structure enables us to obtain an overall mean estimate of the transition probability matrix along with the individual estimates of the weight categories. Through simulations we find that the proposed model is more flexible than hierarchical methods with no partition or fully-pooled alternatives while sacrificing very little efficiency under model misspecification. Applying this method to NGJJ, we found a back-take is the tactic most likely to lead to achieving submission across all weight categories. In addition, we discovered the lightest (66kg) and heaviest (99kg+) weight categories vary significantly from the others in long-term tactical progression.

entry.title: A Review of Bayesian Surrogate Modeling for High-Dimensional Computer Simulations

link.title: A Review of Bayesian Surrogate Modeling for High-Dimensional Computer Simulations

entry.content: Bayesian surrogate models play a central role in the analysis of computationally expensive physics-based simulators, particularly when uncertainty quantification (UQ) is a primary objective. This review provides a high-level overview of commonly used Bayesian surrogate modeling methods for high-dimensional computer simulations, with emphasis on both methodological foundations and practical applications. We review the advantages of Bayesian surrogates, the challenges posed by high-dimensional outputs, and two broad classes of methods: Gaussian process models, including scalable approximations, and Bayesian basis function regression approaches such as polynomial chaos expansions, Bayesian multivariate adaptive regression splines, Bayesian projection pursuit regression, and Bayesian additive regression trees. We also review strategies for handling high-dimensional simulator outputs, of which dimension-reduction approaches based on low-dimensional output representations are most common. Finally, we highlight key applications of Bayesian surrogate modeling in forward UQ, global sensitivity analysis, and Bayesian model calibration, and demonstrate a practical workflow utilizing these methods in simulated and real data analyses. We conclude by identifying open challenges and future research directions related to method selection, computational scalability, predictive accuracy, and UQ fidelity.

entry.title: Bayesian Propensity Score Predictive Inference for Extending Trial Findings to Target Populations

link.title: Bayesian Propensity Score Predictive Inference for Extending Trial Findings to Target Populations

entry.content: The CODIACS Vanguard randomized trial compared a depression care intervention with usual care for patients with persistent depressive symptoms following acute coronary syndrome. We assess whether its findings can be extended to broader patient populations represented by two cohorts constructed from the All of Us electronic health records. This extension is challenging when treatment effects vary across covariates whose distributions differ between trial and target populations. We develop Bayesian Propensity Score Predictive Inference (PSPI), an interaction-based outcome modeling framework that combines Bayesian additive regression trees for potentially high-dimensional covariates with natural cubic splines of the sampling propensity score. Two variants include a separate spline in the treatment effect component alone or in both the prognostic and treatment effect components. The spline components allow separate regularization of selection-related variation and thus improve potential outcome estimation within the observed range and allow an explicit extrapolation rule beyond their boundary knots under substantial covariate shift. An inverse Gumbel transformation of the sampling propensity score balances compression near zero and the extent of extrapolation. Simulation studies show that spline-based PSPI models outperform competing methods in the settings studied, achieving lower root mean squared errors and near-nominal coverage, particularly under substantial covariate shift. In the application, PSPI estimates larger intervention benefits in both target populations than the unadjusted trial estimate.

entry.title: Semiparametric inference for a Target Outcome Leveraging Heterogeneous External Summaries of Auxiliary Outcomes

link.title: Semiparametric inference for a Target Outcome Leveraging Heterogeneous External Summaries of Auxiliary Outcomes

entry.content: The integration of external information can substantially improve the efficiency of statistical inference in an internal study, but is often complicated by between-study heterogeneity. Additional challenges arise when external studies examine auxiliary outcomes rather than on the target outcomes and provide only summary statistics. To address these challenges, we propose a semiparametric framework that incorporates external summary statistics into the internal analysis via the generalized method of moments. To accommodate between-study heterogeneity, the external summaries are formulated within a random-effects model centered on the internal parameter estimates and subsequently embedded into the internal estimating equations. We establish the asymptotic properties of the proposed estimator. While uncertainty from the first-stage estimation vanishes as the number of external studies increases, it remains non-negligible where the number of external studies is moderate. In this setting, we show that a hybrid bootstrap procedure correctly propagates this uncertainty and consistently estimates the asymptotic covariance of the proposed estimator, thereby ensuring valid inference. We further derive theoretical efficiency bounds and demonstrate robust finite-sample performance through simulation studies. In an application to colorectal cancer tumor sequencing data, we show that integrating external information of auxiliary outcomes reveals molecular subtype-specific etiologic associations that would not be detected using the internal data alone.

entry.title: Proportion Outcomes in Interrupted Time Series Analysis: Why Both Boundedness and Autocorrelation Matter

link.title: Proportion Outcomes in Interrupted Time Series Analysis: Why Both Boundedness and Autocorrelation Matter

entry.content: Background: Proportions are common in interrupted time series analysis (ITSA), but bounded outcomes and serial dependence require distinct modeling considerations. This article provides guidance on selecting and evaluating models for proportion outcomes. Methods: Two published healthcare ITSA studies were reanalyzed. The first examined weekly proportions near the boundaries of the unit interval using segmented linear regression. The second examined monthly proportions without reported assessment or adjustment for autocorrelation. Both were reanalyzed using models appropriate for their outcome distributions and temporal dependence. Results: In the first study, segmented linear regression produced six fitted values below zero, and 35 of 66 confidence intervals extended beyond the permissible outcome range. Fractional logistic regression constrained fitted means to the unit interval while accommodating zeros and ones. In the second study, beta autoregressive regression identified significant first-order serial dependence (rho1 = 0.263, 95% CI 0.093 to 0.432; P = .002). After adjustment, residuals showed no evidence of remaining autocorrelation (Ljung-Box Q12 = 15.59; P = .211). Conclusions: Boundedness and serial dependence are distinct considerations in ITSA of proportions. Accounting for autocorrelation does not ensure predictions remain within the permissible range, and modeling bounded outcomes does not ensure serial dependence is addressed. Investigators should assess both features and select models appropriate for the outcome distribution and temporal dependence.

entry.title: Parallel Trends as a Spectrum

link.title: Parallel Trends as a Spectrum

entry.content: Difference-in-differences (DiD) designs are typically used to identify and estimate average causal effects, even though treatment can affect the entire outcome distribution. This has led to a growing interest in distributional DiD methods. However, identifying the full counterfactual distribution requires a parallel trends assumption on the entire distributional dynamics, which can be too strong in practice. We address this problem by introducing a spectrum of identifying restrictions that lie between the average and fully distributional DiD by imposing parallel trends on $L$-moments. This corresponds to a basis expansion of the distributional dynamics. Importantly, each $L$-moment is interpretable as familiar distributional components: location, dispersion, skewness, kurtosis, etc. Researchers can pick and choose which features they want to target. For example, the second $L$-moment identifies the Gini mean difference, but does not require imposing mean-level or higher-order parallel trends. Taking a collection of $L$-moments can approximate distributional dynamics under weaker conditions since it leaves untargeted components unrestricted. We develop conditions under which higher-order $L$-moments decay, efficient estimators, and simultaneous inference across growing collections of moments. We demonstrate the benefits of our framework by exploring distributional changes to healthcare spending after the rollout of Medicare Part D.

entry.title: Fitting Dynamic Conditional Densities to Cross-Sectional Returns with Persistent Tail Intensities

link.title: Fitting Dynamic Conditional Densities to Cross-Sectional Returns with Persistent Tail Intensities

entry.content: We propose dynamic conditional densities with spline mixtures (DCD-SM) to detect whether the tail intensity of financial returns depends on past information after accounting for volatility and tail-order dynamics. The target is a weighted mixture of the conditional return densities of individual assets in a cross section. Individual distributions may differ, and returns within a date may be dependent. A normalized spline-mixture correction uses score-driven updates to change left and right tail intensities while preserving the reference tail order. We use Wald tests for persistence and assess empirical size, power, and forecast stability in simulations. With fitted references that have dynamic tail order, Wald tests at the nominal five-percent level detect dynamics that affect both tail intensities in the same direction in all 19 US and Japanese equity cross sections, for both raw returns and residuals after principal-component removal with training-fixed loadings. Evidence for dynamics in the imbalance between the two tail intensities is more limited. In the residuals, the correction improves out-of-sample one-percent lower-tail quantile loss relative to these references in 16 of 19 panels, with three significant positive differences at the five-percent level. Forecast gains are most evident in log scores and one-percent quantile losses and are less uniform for five-percent quantile loss.

entry.title: Higher Order Asymptotics of Regression Adjustment Estimators for Causal Inference

link.title: Higher Order Asymptotics of Regression Adjustment Estimators for Causal Inference

entry.content: Regression adjustment is widely used to improve the precision of average treatment effect estimates from randomized controlled trials. Interacted regression weakly dominates simple regression in terms of its first-order behavior but, in 50-50 randomized trials, the asymptotic variance of both methods is the same and so relative performance is determined by higher-order behavior. Here, we conduct a higher order analysis to compare simple vs. interacted regression adjustments in the equal-probability case. The relative performance of the methods depends on a number of factors including feature skewness, treatment-effect heterogeneity, heteroskedasticity, and nonlinear misspecification, and can favor either estimator. However, in some practically important settings, including when features are skewed and outlying feature values are associated with higher outcome noise, simple regression can outperform interacted regression by a material amount.

entry.title: When Statisticians Can Also Be AI Engineers, What Could We Build?

link.title: When Statisticians Can Also Be AI Engineers, What Could We Build?

entry.content: Statistical software makes methods widely available. Good statistical work, however, often requires conversations that clarify the scientific question, how the data were collected, and what conclusions the evidence can support. Coding agents and reusable AI infrastructure create opportunities for statisticians to incorporate these processes into agentic tools for research, practice, and education. A review of agentic AI applications for data analysis and study design distinguishes general human participation from human interaction guided by statistical principles. We examine how statistical expertise can guide the design and evaluation of domain-specific interactive harnesses. Two practical entry points illustrate how statisticians can begin building: an implemented causal-consulting skill within an existing agent environment and Model Forge, a custom harness for interactive model and algorithm development. These design examples connect statistical principles to choices about context, memory, tools, and interfaces, and motivate evaluation of both computational correctness and the scientific consequences of interaction. We conclude with a broader interdisciplinary research agenda on adaptive human-agent interaction, including selective information acquisition, evolving user preferences, and evaluation under uncertainty.

entry.title: Finite-horizon maintenance under geometric-process models: Quantifying model and decision uncertainty

link.title: Finite-horizon maintenance under geometric-process models: Quantifying model and decision uncertainty

entry.content: Geometric process (GP) models are widely used for repairable systems whose inter-failure times evolve over successive failure-repair cycles. Maintenance decisions under GP models are often made with limited failure data and are subject to uncertainty in baseline selection and the resulting maintenance decision. Existing approaches typically rely on model ranking and plug-in estimates, which can understate uncertainty surrounding next-cycle replacement decisions. This paper develops a unified generalized-inference framework for finite-horizon, event-driven maintenance decision making under GP models. The proposed framework quantifies uncertainty in GP model parameters, cycle-specific reliability, hazard rate, one-cycle cost rate, and the associated optimal replacement time. For exponential and gamma baselines, the framework yields generalized confidence intervals through generalized pivotal quantities. For the Weibull baseline, it is implemented through a generalized fiducial approach. It also extends to a finite-sample discrimination procedure for quantifying baseline-selection uncertainty. Theoretical results establish the asymptotic validity of the proposed procedures and their interval estimates. Simulation study shows reliable finite-sample coverage for model parameters and nonlinear maintenance-relevant quantities, and satisfactory discrimination performance. A case study on aircraft air-conditioning failures shows that, in early cycles, replacement schedules with similar expected cost can imply materially different risk profiles, so a single plug-in recommendation may be misleading.

entry.title: Bias-aware meta-analysis: beyond fixed-effect and random-effects meta-analyses

link.title: Bias-aware meta-analysis: beyond fixed-effect and random-effects meta-analyses

entry.content: Meta-analysis aims to synthesize multiple studies to obtain a summary estimate of a population parameter of interest. However, existing meta-analysis methods require strong assumptions that render them not robust to bias and heterogeneity of the studies. In particular, fixed-effect meta-analysis assumes a common parameter across the studies, whereas random-effects meta-analysis models heterogeneity as independent and identically distributed random effects, which still implies a common parameter marginally over the random effects. Due to their limitations, we propose a bias-aware meta-analysis framework that allows for heterogeneous studies with fixed, unknown biases. With no bias, our bias-aware meta-analysis reduces to fixed-effect meta-analysis; with a given bound on the bias, we can still use the fixed-effect meta-analysis point estimator and standard error, but we must inflate the critical value for confidence intervals from the standard normal quantile to a folded normal quantile. We recommend reporting the maximum bias for significance, the maximum value of the bias such that the confidence intervals exclude the null value. We propose a formal model checking procedure and recommend reporting the minimum bias for compatibility, the minimum value of the bias such that the bias-aware meta-analysis model is compatible with the observed data. We discuss the practical implementation of our method and, in particular, the approaches to calibrating the maximum bias for significance. We also compare our method with traditional fixed-effect and random-effects meta-analyses.

entry.title: Asymptotic spectral properties and extreme eigenvalues of sample correlation matrices from nonstationary high-dimensional VAR processes

link.title: Asymptotic spectral properties and extreme eigenvalues of sample correlation matrices from nonstationary high-dimensional VAR processes

entry.content: We study the limiting spectral distribution and extreme eigenvalues of the sample correlation matrix $\hat{\boldsymbol{R}}$ from a high-dimensional vector autoregressive (VAR) processes. Depending on whether roots of the characteristic polynomial of given VAR lie on (nonstationary) or outside (super-nonstationary) the unit circle, $\hat{\boldsymbol{R}}$ presents different types of asymptotic spectral properties. Under both nonstationary and super-nonstationary regimes, the empirical spectral distribution of $\hat{\boldsymbol{R}}$ degenerates in probability to a point mass at zero. The rescaled extreme eigenvalues of $\hat{\boldsymbol{R}}$ are asymptotically equivalent to the eigenvalues of a finite-dimensional symmetric random matrix determined by the characteristic roots. Moreover, under super-nonstationarity, $\hat{\boldsymbol{R}}$ degenerates in probability to a matrix with finite rank.

entry.title: Mapping Academic Sports Analytics: A Content Analysis of JQAS and JSA

link.title: Mapping Academic Sports Analytics: A Content Analysis of JQAS and JSA

entry.content: Sports analytics has expanded rapidly in professional sports and mainstream culture, yet defining its academic core remains a challenge. In this paper, we provide an empirical map of the academic sports analytics landscape based on a systematic content analysis of approximately 700 papers published in two leading dedicated journals, the Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports (JQAS) and the Journal of Sports Analytics (JSA), between the years 2005 and 2024. We classify each paper by sport discipline, mathematical method, and core research area, identify recurring themes, and examine macro trends. We find game tactics, player evaluation, team ranking, result forecasting, and tournament design to be the most studied research areas in sports analytics. We highlight selected papers in each area, illustrating the wide range of mathematical methods used and sports disciplines analyzed. Our work offers a comprehensive overview of the questions, methods, and disciplines that characterize the field, serving as a foundational reference for practitioners and researchers in sports analytics.

entry.title: Honest Inference for Synthetic Controls with Imperfect Fit: Time-Split Validity and the Choice of Anchor

link.title: Honest Inference for Synthetic Controls with Imperfect Fit: Time-Split Validity and the Choice of Anchor

entry.content: Synthetic controls are used for one treated unit that lies outside its donors’ range, with a pre-treatment window too short for residual-based standard errors to be trusted. We propose inference that separates the periods used to fit the synthetic control from the periods used to assess its error. Weights are fitted on an early block of pre-treatment periods, and the gap on a later block calibrates the bias and the noise. The resulting interval has finite-sample coverage under an explicit restriction on how far the counterfactual may depart from the extrapolated pre-treatment gap, for any fitting rule that uses only the early block. The leading restriction bounds the curvature of the gap and leaves its slope free, and the breakdown curvature at which the interval first includes zero states how much extrapolation a conclusion needs. We show when drift bounds calibrated from donor placebos are valid and how to allow for serial dependence. In simulations, conventional intervals undercover when the treated unit drifts from its donors, while the proposed interval covers whenever its restriction holds and the noise is serially independent. Re-analyses of three classic applications show that some well-known conclusions rest on far stronger extrapolation than others.

link.title: Partial Identification of Survival Prediction Performance under Dependent Right Censoring

entry.content: Survival prediction models are usually evaluated under right censoring by inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW), which assumes independent censoring, an assumption that cannot generally be verified from right-censored data. Leaving the dependence between event and censoring times unrestricted, we derive sharp bounds on the integrated Brier score (IBS) of a fixed model and on IBS differences between models by partial identification. The bounds use the fact that each individual’s event time is shared across evaluation times and models, and for more than two models we also derive the sharp upper bound on the difference from the best competitor. A negative upper bound on a difference shows that one model has a smaller IBS than the other under every full-data distribution compatible with the observed data. For a fixed observed-data distribution, we develop estimators, confidence regions, a test of robust strict dominance, and an intersection-union test. In simulations, the confidence regions and pairwise tests performed close to their nominal levels. In three applications, the tests supported the IPCW ranking only for mortgage prepayment data with little censoring, whereas for the other two data sets the observed data alone did not support it.

entry.title: Random Jump Forests

link.title: Random Jump Forests

entry.content: Random jump forests are introduced as a nonparametric tool for estimating conditional cumulative transition rates and occupation probabilities in multi-state models. The main idea is that a single tree partitions the covariate space for all transitions simultaneously, using partially observed trajectories, and with Nelson–Aalen estimators at the terminal nodes. Occupation probabilities are recovered through the product integral without requiring the Markov assumption. entry.title: Direct Simulation of Poisson and Newton Kernel Distributions

link.title: Direct Simulation of Poisson and Newton Kernel Distributions

entry.content: The Poisson kernel-based (PKB) distribution is a flexible and numerically convenient family on the unit sphere used for model-based clustering, uniformity testing, and directional data analysis. We show that none is needed. A uniformly random line through the interior point $\rho\mu$ meets the sphere in two points; selecting one with probability proportional to the opposite segment length returns exactly the target density. The sampler is exact, rejection- and tuning-free, uses one uniform direction and one Bernoulli draw, and costs $O(d)$ operations. We place the distribution in the power-Saw family of densities proportional to $|x-\rho\mu|^{-\xi}$ and show that, for $d\geq3$, the same construction is exact for one further exponent. This introduces the Newton kernel-based (NKB) distribution, whose normalizing constant is identically one. Across a wide grid of dimensions, concentrations, and sample sizes, the direct sampler is faster than the better of two previously recommended methods in every case, with the largest gains at moderate concentration.

entry.title: Trend-concordance grey incidence with likelinesses closed-form small-sample inference without elicited prior densities

link.title: Trend-concordance grey incidence with likelinesses closed-form small-sample inference without elicited prior densities

entry.content: Grey incidence analysis ranks the factors of a system from short sequences without assuming a probability model, but the grade it returns has no sampling theory: nothing indicates whether an ordering reflects the system or the few data at hand. This paper reduces trend agreement between two sequences to the signs of their centred increments and analyses the resulting counts with Lovegrove’s likelinesses, averages of probabilities over an underlying set of distributions that replace the elicitation of a prior density by a statement of what is possible. The result is a concordance incidence grade with closed-form inference: estimation, the likeliness that one factor outranks another, prediction of future concordance and a baseline for searches over many candidates, with bounded underlying sets encoding partial knowledge. Comparisons whose sign falls below the resolution of the data are treated as indeterminate; discarding them is exact when they carry no information, and otherwise the grade becomes a grey number whose width measures what the data cannot decide. The grade is symmetric in any system and resolves the conflict between the totality and pair-symmetry axioms by moving system dependence into inference. Simulations show that plug-in prediction underestimates variance by a factor of up to 1 + m/n regardless of sample size, and that a fair-coin baseline yields up to 63% spurious patterns in searches, where a correctly bounded set keeps them below 5%. Worked textbook examples and a regularisation benchmark with known truth illustrate the method.

link.title: Acquisition for Spherical-Linear Bayesian Optimization on the Cube

entry.content: Recent work demonstrated that executing Bayesian Optimization (BO) using simply a linear surrogate with a clever transformation is enough to approximate the performance of the standard Gaussian-Process (GP) based version on high-dimensional test functions. When the decision region is a sphere, this strategy admits rapid exact acquisition. However, it is the unit cube we encounter most often in the BO literature, and in this setting a standard approach, namely a multi-start quasi-Newton method, is employed for solving the acquisition subproblem. In this article, we will discuss a series of results, both positive and negative, regarding the complexity of global resolution of various acquisition subproblems over the unit cube. On the basis of this discussion, we will propose a new acquisition function which is globally optimizable using significantly less execution time than the incumbent approach while maintaining or improving performance. The resulting method is competitive with GP-based BO in terms of accuracy per evaluation, and is superior in terms of accuracy per walltime on black-boxes of low to moderate computational intensity.

entry.title: Sparse Bayesian Neural Networks via Sticky Piecewise Deterministic Markov Processes

link.title: Sparse Bayesian Neural Networks via Sticky Piecewise Deterministic Markov Processes

entry.content: There is growing evidence that the performance of a neural network depends largely on a small subset of its weights, which are typically identified by training a dense network and pruning it afterwards. Within a Bayesian framework, pruning can be directly incorporated through a spike-and-slab prior, providing a proper treatment of the uncertainties involved, both with respect to pruning and to parameter uncertainty. In Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), sampling by MCMC is notoriously hard. We demonstrate that modern Monte Carlo methods based on piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) can be used to sample posteriors of BNNs asymptotically exact whenever numerically constructed rate bounds hold. Spike-and-slab priors can be incorporated through sticky versions of the PDMPs, setting weights exactly to zero during sampling. We examine the predictive performance and convergence of the samplers, and show that sparse BNNs sampled this way can be more robust to input noise than dense ones.

entry.title: Resampling-Based Inference for Incomplete Paired Functional Data

link.title: Resampling-Based Inference for Incomplete Paired Functional Data

entry.content: We consider testing equality of mean functions for paired functional data, where one entire function is missing. To use all available information from the paired and unpaired observations, we propose globalized test statistics that are based on a weighted sum of point-wise paired-$t$ and Welch-$t$-type statistics. By the use of empirical process theory, we derive the asymptotic limit distributions of the resulting test statistics under the null hypothesis and show consistency against fixed alternatives. As they are non-pivotal and contain complex dependencies from the paired and incomplete observations, a permutation and parametric bootstrap procedures is proposed to compute critical values. The work includes a theoretical investigation of the asymptotic behaviour of the two resampling approaches and state regularity conditions under which the corresponding resampling tests are valid. Simulation studies show that the proposed methods provide accurate type I error control and competitive power for most settings under study. An illustrative analysis of functional emission data demonstrates the applicability of the methods.

entry.title: Out-of-sample prediction in SEM: A simulation-based comparison of maximum likelihood and (consistent) partial least squares

link.title: Out-of-sample prediction in SEM: A simulation-based comparison of maximum likelihood and (consistent) partial least squares

entry.content: Structural equation modeling (SEM) is widely used to study relationships among unobserved constructs. Over recent years, the interest in computing predictions with SEM has grown. Different prediction procedures have been proposed for this purpose, including MLpredict, which is based on maximum likelihood (ML) estimation, and PLS(c)predict, which is based on partial least squares (PLS). The out-of-sample predictive performances of these procedures have not yet been compared. In our work, we conduct a comprehensive Monte Carlo study to compare out-of-sample predictions of MLpredict and PLS(c)predict for indicators associated with endogenous constructs, so-called operative predictions. Here, we vary key design factors regarding, for instance, the strengths of structural relations, the training sample size, and the construct types in the data generating processes, which determine the presence or absence of construct misspecification. Across the investigated conditions, MLpredict and PLS(c)predict exhibit similar predictive performance according to two assessment criteria, indicating that neither procedure is uniformly superior for operative prediction. Out-of-sample predictive performance is driven mainly by the strength of the relations between the variables, whereas training sample size and construct misspecification have comparatively little influence on it. An exception is the occasionally inflated prediction error of PLScpredict, which is in line with previous findings for ordinal indicators. Overall, our results suggest that, in the studied setting, fine-grained methodological differences between traditional SEM and PLS-based procedures matter less for out-of-sample predictive performance than properties of the data generating process, such as the coefficient of determination of endogenous constructs.

entry.title: Mixed Engression: Distributional Regression for Multivariate Mixed-Type Responses

link.title: Mixed Engression: Distributional Regression for Multivariate Mixed-Type Responses

entry.content: Estimating the conditional distribution of multivariate responses with continuous and binary components requires capturing their dependence, respecting their different supports, and accommodating potentially heavy-tailed continuous outcomes. We propose mixed engression, which fits a continuous generator using energy losses induced by bounded discrepancies and then thresholds its soft binary outputs to produce mixed-response samples. Because the discrepancies are bounded, the population objective remains well defined without response-moment assumptions. However, we show that the full-response energy distance for the complete response vector can tend to zero before thresholding yet remain bounded away from zero afterward as response dimensions grow. A separate energy loss on the entire binary vector captures discrepancies obscured by the full-response comparison and controls the effect of thresholding. The generator is therefore fitted using an augmented energy loss that combines the full-response and binary components. Under compositional smoothness of the structural functions and a uniform threshold-margin condition, we derive nonasymptotic bounds on the final sampler’s full-response error for sparse ReLU estimators of models driven by Gaussian or Student-t structural noise, yielding polynomial convergence rates up to logarithmic factors. We also establish consistency when the covariate, response, and noise dimensions grow under suitable conditions. Simulations show improved accuracy relative to the comparison methods under the full-response energy distance, including in heavy-tailed settings. Moderate binary augmentation substantially improves binary-distribution accuracy while largely preserving full-response accuracy.

entry.title: Fréchet Kriging for Metric Space-Valued Spatial Data

link.title: Fréchet Kriging for Metric Space-Valued Spatial Data

entry.content: Spatial prediction of non-Euclidean data, such as probability distributions, symmetric positive definite matrices, and networks, arises in many modern applications. Such data are naturally modeled as elements of general metric spaces, where classical kriging methods that rely on vector space structure are no longer directly applicable. We introduce Fr'echet kriging, a general framework for spatial prediction of metric space-valued data. Fr'echet kriging replaces the weighted average in classical ordinary kriging with a weighted Fr'echet mean, while the weights are determined by characterizing the spatial dependence structure through a generalized variogram. This construction allows the proposed method to preserve the intrinsic geometry of the response space without requiring an embedding into a linear space. We establish theoretical properties of the proposed predictor, including a surrogate optimality property and consistency under variogram misspecification for a fixed working variogram under suitable regularity conditions. Simulation studies for univariate distributions and symmetric positive definite matrices demonstrate favorable predictive performance compared with existing approaches. We further illustrate the practical utility of the proposed framework through applications to exceedance probabilities of daily average temperatures, joint probability densities of daily minimum and maximum temperatures, and inter-industry monetary flow networks.

link.title: Computation of Maximum Likelihood Estimates for Multiresponse Generalized Linear Mixed Models with Non-nested, Correlated Random Effects

entry.content: Estimation of generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) with non-nested random effects structures requires approximation of high-dimensional integrals. Many existing methods are tailored to the low-dimensional integrals produced by nested designs. We explore the modifications that are required in order to adapt an EM algorithm with first-order and fully exponential Laplace approximations to a non-nested, multiple response model. The equations in the estimation routine are expressed as functions of the first four derivatives of the conditional log likelihood of an arbitrary GLMM, providing a template for future applications. We apply the method to a joint Poisson-binary model for ranking sporting teams, and discuss the estimation of a correlated random effects model designed to evaluate the sensitivity of value-added models for teacher evaluation to assumptions about the missing data process. Source code in R is provided in the online supplementary material.

entry.title: A Diagnostic for Bias in Linear Mixed Model Estimators Induced by Dependence Between the Random Effects and the Corresponding Model Matrix

link.title: A Diagnostic for Bias in Linear Mixed Model Estimators Induced by Dependence Between the Random Effects and the Corresponding Model Matrix

entry.content: We explore how violations of the often-overlooked standard assumption that the random effects model matrix in a linear mixed model is fixed (and thus independent of the random effects vector) can lead to bias in estimators of estimable functions of the fixed effects. However, if the random effects of the original mixed model are instead also treated as fixed effects, or if the fixed and random effects model matrices are orthogonal with respect to the inverse of the error covariance matrix (with probability one), or if the random effects and the corresponding model matrix are independent, then these estimators are unbiased. The bias in the general case is quantified, and a diagnostic for its random-effects contribution is compared to a randomized permutation distribution of the predicted random effects, producing an informative summary graphic for each estimator of interest. This is demonstrated through the examination of sporting outcomes used to estimate a home field advantage.

link.title: Inference on Quantile Treatment Effects with Small Treatment Groups

entry.content: We develop inference for conditional quantile treatment effects that allows treatment groups to remain small as the overall sample grows. Such groups arise naturally in multivalued treatment models. Our procedure combines estimation of a conditional quantile function from a large reference group with an exact conditional Bernoulli representation of quantile indicators. We establish asymptotic size control and derive a power bound allowing treatment-group sizes to remain bounded. The framework accommodates nonseparable outcome functions, heteroskedasticity, and flexible error distributions across treatment profiles. We illustrate its scope through dynamic treatment models, nonseparable quantile models, and difference-in-differences designs with staggered adoption. Monte Carlo experiments assess finite-sample performance, and an application to temperature shocks and GDP growth illustrates inference on effects associated with distinct treatment histories.

link.title: The Anatomy of Dependence in Multivariate Ordered Choice

entry.content: When individuals make simultaneous decisions across multiple ordered dimensions, standard multivariate ordered choice models impose narrow bracketing, with each dimension decided as if the others did not exist. We develop a general rectangular structure model capturing broad bracketing while nesting the standard model. The framework introduces two layers of dependence, one through the threshold structure associated with decision rules and the other through the correlation of latent utilities. We provide microfoundations, prove identification, and discuss estimation. We showcase the model in applications to parental investment in children’s education, cryptocurrency familiarity and expectations, and health insurance, where the latter separates moral hazard from adverse selection.
